title: 1 Samuel 13:16–23
context: 1 Samuel 13:16–23 describes Israel’s weakness before the Philistines. Saul and Jonathan hold Geba with their small force, while Philistine raiding parties go out from Michmash in three directions. The narrator explains that the Philistines had prevented the Israelites from having blacksmiths, so Israel depended on them even to sharpen farming tools, and in the day of battle only Saul and Jonathan had sword and spear. A WEB footnote explains the payim, the fee charged for sharpening. The section highlights how unequal the conflict was and prepares for the LORD’s deliverance through Jonathan in chapter 14.

verses.text: Saul, and Jonathan his son, and the people who were present with them, stayed in Geba of Benjamin; but the Philistines encamped in Michmash.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul, Jonathan and the people stay in Geba, while the Philistines camp at Michmash. Arminian readers note that the two forces face each other across a short distance, with Israel vastly outnumbered and Saul now carrying the weight of Samuel’s rebuke.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrative now pairs Saul and Jonathan, preparing for the contrast between them in chapter 14. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple setting of the scene, and neither finds a doctrinal question in it.

verses.text: The raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies: one company turned to the way that leads to Ophrah, to the land of Shual;
verses.arminianNotes: Raiders come out of the Philistine camp in three companies, one toward Ophrah and the land of Shual. Arminian readers note that the raids show the Philistines’ freedom to plunder Israel’s territory, while Israel’s army can do little to stop them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the raids underline the oppression from which God had promised Saul would deliver his people (9:16). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative’s portrait of Israel’s helplessness before the Philistines, which makes the coming deliverance more striking.

verses.text: another company turned the way to Beth Horon; and another company turned the way of the border that looks down on the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The other companies go toward Beth Horon and toward the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim. Arminian readers note that the Philistines spread out across the land, confident in their superiority, a picture of the pressure under which Israel lived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the geographical detail grounds the account in real places and shows the Philistines controlling routes in several directions. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the description of the raids, and neither finds a theological contrast in it.

verses.text: Now there was no blacksmith found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, “Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears”;
verses.arminianNotes: There was “no blacksmith found throughout all the land of Israel,” because the Philistines feared the Hebrews would make swords or spears. Arminian readers note the deliberate policy of disarmament. Israel’s weakness was not only military but economic and technological.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the policy left Israel dependent on its oppressors, a condition that made any victory all the more clearly God’s work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical background that explains the scarcity of weapons in 13:22, and both see it heightening the drama of chapter 14.

verses.text: but all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, each man to sharpen his own plowshare, mattock, ax, and sickle.
verses.arminianNotes: The Israelites have to go down to the Philistines “to sharpen his own plowshare, mattock, ax, and sickle.” Arminian readers note the humiliation of depending on the enemy for basic farm work, a daily reminder of Israel’s subjection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the dependence touches ordinary life, not only warfare, showing how deeply the Philistine oppression reached. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the background of Israel’s weakness, preparing for the LORD’s deliverance, which does not depend on weapons (compare 17:47).

verses.text: The price was one payim each to sharpen mattocks, plowshares, pitchforks, axes, and goads.
verses.arminianNotes: “The price was one payim each to sharpen mattocks, plowshares, pitchforks, axes, and goads.” A WEB footnote explains that a payim (or pim) was 2/3 shekel of silver, about 7.6 grams or 0.26 ounces. Arminian readers note the economic burden this placed on Israel’s farmers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the detail adds historical texture and underlines the cost of Israel’s dependence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as background, and both use the WEB footnote to explain the payim, without drawing theological conclusions from the figure.

verses.text: So it came to pass in the day of battle that neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of any of the people who were with Saul and Jonathan; but Saul and Jonathan his son had them.
verses.arminianNotes: In the day of battle, “neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of any of the people who were with Saul and Jonathan; but Saul and Jonathan his son had them.” Arminian readers note the vulnerability of the army. Only the king and his son are armed, a striking setup for what Jonathan will do with the LORD’s help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the scarcity of weapons sets the stage for a victory that clearly belongs to God, as David later declares: “the LORD doesn’t save with sword and spear” (17:47). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for chapter 14, where the LORD saves Israel through a few.

verses.text: The garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.
verses.arminianNotes: “The garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.” Arminian readers note that this outpost becomes the target of Jonathan’s daring venture in 14:1. The narrative moves from description to action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse forms a bridge to Jonathan’s exploit, placing the Philistine garrison at the pass. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a narrative transition, and neither finds a doctrinal point of difference in it.
